citations.review_text: IM really mad i bought this... I uninstalled and reinstalled on both consoles and have the same problem. I always loved skyrim and wanted to love this, but it doesn't seem like it was meant to be.

0/10 First Impression. Absolutely Unacceptable.

Forty-three minutes. That's how long I spent trying to play a game I had already paid for.

The experience went like this: install, launch, crash, repair files, launch again, crash, repair again, finally reach the title screen, get sent to create an online account and accept legal agreements, return to the game... and it crashes again. Then the launcher tells me to repair the files yet again.

I repaired the installation multiple times. It made absolutely no difference.

The only part of this entire process that worked flawlessly was taking my money. After that I was immediately pushed toward creating another account, accepting additional agreements, being introduced to a subscription service, and exposed to in-game microtransactions before I could even play. Meanwhile, the actual game couldn't stay running long enough to let me create a character.

This is one of the worst first impressions I've had in years. A game should work before it starts asking me for subscriptions and additional purchases.

If your launcher's solution to every crash is "repair the game files," even after repeated successful repairs, then your launcher isn't diagnosing the problem—it's wasting the player's time.

I wanted to enjoy this game. Instead, I spent nearly an hour troubleshooting software I had just installed. That's not entertainment; it's unpaid technical support.

Fix your launcher. Fix your crash handling. Let people actually play the game they purchased before trying to sell them anything else.

The game is great, one of my top 5 MMO's.  What people say about the monetization is very true, a lot of spots that make you feel that push to sub or buy content.  I would say character classes/builds feeling kind of samish would be a weakness.  Story is really strong in a lot of places, really enjoyed a lot of the zone stories and quests.  Did not do enough PvP to offer a rating for that side.

Game is 4/5,  3/5 if monetization bothers you.

The Crown Store kills it for me.  You can earn the cosmetics slowly without paying, but if you want new quests, companions, and story, you have to get ESO+ or try to get other players to buy them for you for gold.  I'd only recommend this to people who don't mind a monthly sub style MMO, because ESO+ unlocks most of that stuff as long as you stay subbed as well as some major inventory QOL features that are obviously only locked to make it harder to be F2P after buying the base game.

The Elder Scrolls Online proves that you don't need to play a single-player Elder Scrolls game to get lost in Tamriel for hundreds of hours.

The world is massive, and the best part is that almost every location feels worth exploring. From ancient ruins and mysterious caves to beautiful cities and dangerous landscapes, ESO captures the feeling of adventure that made the series famous. 🗺️✨

The freedom is incredible. You can become a warrior, mage, assassin, healer, crafter, treasure hunter, or something completely different. The class system, skill lines, crafting, housing, and countless quests give you endless ways to customize your character. 🛡️🧙

The storytelling is surprisingly strong for an MMO. Many quests feel personal, with memorable characters and fully voiced dialogue that makes the world feel alive. The ability to explore almost all of Tamriel with friends is a huge bonus. 🤝

The amount of content can be overwhelming, the combat may feel simple compared with traditional action RPGs, and some of the best features are locked behind expansions or subscriptions. Still, the sheer amount of things to do makes it one of the most complete MMORPG experiences available. ⭐

I started with a simple quest. 200 hours later I was decorating a house, crafting gear, stealing from NPCs, and still finding new places on the map. 😂🏰

Tamriel is huge. Bring snacks. 🍻

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the combat system as lacking depth, feeling simplistic, or relying on pressing buttons from a limited skill bar.

citations.review_text: A sterile wooden world. Combat is lifeless and the environments feel empty. The ui interface reflects the blandness of the game also. Most encounters are easy wins and pose no challenge. Story and voice acting are the only thing decent about the game.

If you're looking for an Oblivion, Skyrim or Fallout game... you're not going to get it here.

The game is in NO WAY BAD. But, it lacks the oomph and freedom you would get in other TES titles. This has a multiplayer sheen to it. Skills are performed at the press of a button from a skill bar. You can't spontaneously murder random people and face the consequences of doing so.

It lacks in all the broken Bethesda ways.

If you're an avid MMORPG player, you may enjoy this. But if you're looking to character build and go on an epic quest where you feel like YOU ARE YOUR CHARACTER - you're better off modding Skyrim.

Sorry TESO, I really wanted to enjoy this more.

Alright, I'm going to be honest with you all: This is not a good game. If you are a massive Elder Scrolls fan, this game becomes OKAY AT BEST. Otherwise, it is not an MMO worth your time or money even on sale. Yes there's no monthly payment required to play (the Plus Membership is for extra content) which is great, but as an RPG it is just not very fun. 

The quest dialogue is all voiced but your character goes out of view, which takes you out if you play in third person. The writing is terrible, often times I read the dialogue choices and thought "what a dumb thing for my character to ask", and would try to continue the quest without asking but the game won't let you continue until you ask it. Compare it to a game like Star Wars The Old Republic where every class story arc is interesting and your characters are allowed to have cool moments within cutscenes. The gameplay sucks, the simple joy of seeing your skill bar progressively get bigger and start taking up your screen on the vertical right side is gone. You get 5 active skills + 1 ultimate, at level 15 you get a second set of 5 + 1. But guess what, if you are a sorcerer for example and summon a minion on one bar, then switch to the other bar mid combat to use your skills there, the game will kill your minion even if it's full health. Great. Thanks, game. This was all done to make the game play well on consoles apparently. 

So yeah, tons of content but none of it particularly amazing besides the occasional Elder Scrolls reference you recognize. And the community is not anything to write home about either, pretty standard online game community, no one is going out of their way to interact with each other in any meaningful way, if you wanna join a guild you get told to join a discord. If you want an online game to grind there are plenty of other options.

The combat is boring. It can be summed up as walk over to a enemy and activate abilities until there health bar goes down to 0. You don't even need to aim, and projectiles home in on a target so they can't be dodged.
The classes, the skills and the combat felt lackluster. It literally made me uninstall and asked for a refund which I immediately got.

citations.review_text: I'm enjoying this game with my wife. It's an above average MMO if you're used to games like WoW or Guild Wars 2. Okay as long as you like to inventory management

Honestly a real fun game. I bought ESO (with all the DLCs on Steam) when it was on sale, and at first I didn't think I'd enjoy it that much, because I prefer singleplayer games, but I was pleasantly surprised to find that I really enjoy playing.

That said, it does have some downsides. ESO+ is basically a must-have. Okay sure, you can play without it, but inventory management will be a genuine nightmare beyond what you may be thinking. ESO without ESO+ is only for people who enjoy constant back-and-forth for hours on end.

Also, bear in mind that, even if you buy the game with all the DLCs on Steam, you still don't have access to all in-game content. There are a significant lot of regions that are stuck behind DLCs you either buy in the in-game store with Crowns (a currency you buy on Steam for the game), which is the very expensive option, or by having ESO+ - but the latter means that if you drop ESO+, you no longer have access to those DLCs. It's kinda BS all around.

So... I think the game still earns a solid 7/10. Frankly, gameplay wise it's arguably a 10/10, but the annoying financial choices for this game drop it to a 7 for me. If that's not an issue to you, then I doubt you'll find anything to complain about this game!
The base game should be free, if there is a paid subscription! Compare ESO to SWTOR or Warframe or anything else, really. Also, the Crafting Bag requires ESO+, which is not cool.

I'm a veteran of the WoW, Guild Wars, and Destiny communities and this is still my favorite MMO of all time.  
Some of my favorite things are:
1) Unlike GW2, ESO's megaservers ensure every map feels so alive and populated, I love constantly seeing other players on their adventures, especially in the cities and so forth. 
2) The voice acting is always phenomenal and immersive. Engaging from the first moment you enter the universe.
3) Queueing for group content feels easy and low pressure, even in early-game stages. Unlike the LFG systems in other games where I often felt like too much of a noob to try, the ESO dungeon finder system tends to foster an attitude of "anyone can give it a go"
4) On the other hand, group activities are truly optional. If I want to focus on single-player experience, I love playing ESO like I'm playing Skyrim. Spending time exploring the environment, reading lore books, and talking to NPCs. 
5) The amount of content is just mind boggling. At 1000 hours, there are still zones I have never completed the main storyline for.
6) The housing system and decorating is next level. It truly is like a completely second game within this game.

My main qualm is the pricing model and the ESO plus access to the crafting bag. If you want to do ANY crafting in this game, you need ESO plus in order to store mats. I wish they would rethink this particular aspect of ESO plus. It has acted as a barrier for several friends who have played for a while and then put the game down because they wanted to go deeper into crafting but didn't want to pay the subscription. I'm just a girly pop, what can I say, but I want more colorful mounts and ways to accessorize beyond what exists already. I know they try to stay lore-friendly and all... but sometimes a girl just w…

Its no masterpiece but its very enjoyable for what it is, each zone has its own self contained story, the companions are enjoyable enough even though they can get annopying after you hear the same voicelines 1000 times but you can turn it off, the cash shop is horribly over priced but thats every game these days unfortunately, if you want to get into crafting then the monthly sub is a must have since the craft bag is locked in it which is dumb, the trials and dungeons are fun and unique, the classes vary enough to keep things fresh and its overall its worth the entry cost and who knows maybe you will get lost in the world

To start: ESO Has an amazing world, solid voice acting, and one of the most casual-friendly MMO combat setups I've played.

The problem is that almost every system is built around friction:

-Inventory management is absolutely miserable without ESO+.

-The UI is so lacking that addons are essentially mandatory. I considered a minimap addon essential within my first week.

-The game constantly buries information behind unintuitive awkward menus. I spent a solid 10 minutes trying to figure out how to leave a dungeon group.

-Questing is often incoherent. Major characters can appear alive, dead, or meeting you for the "first time" depending on which storyline you happen to be playing. It is very jarring and breaks immersion.

-Progression becomes increasingly about grinding currencies, collections, achievements and champion points (CP). Notice the absence of "gear" on that list. More on that later.

-Endgame optimization effectively expects constant weapon/bar swapping to maintain buffs and access your full toolkit.

-The "solution" is spending dozens of hours grinding Antiquities for Oakensoul, a ring that removes bar swapping by limiting you to a single six-button action bar. I'll be honest, I had choice words for ESO over both the swapping and the "fix".

-Gear progression eventually becomes shockingly horizontal for the average MMO player used to continued vertical gear progression. Once you've assembled a competent endgame build, future upgrades often feel like minor percentage increases rather than exciting power spikes, and these are very few and far between.

I reached 500+ CP, completed all 3 alliance storylines as well as several DLC stories, acquired Oakensoul, capped all tradeskills and have most of my tradeskill trait research done, fully geared my character in build appropriate legendary sets, and was soloing dungeons and world bosses without difficulty. 

Then I realized there wasn't much left except making numbers slightly bigger via CP grinding or coll…

Headline: 1600+ hours in. The slow decline of a giant, and what it desperately needs to survive.With over 1,655 hours registered on Steam (and many more outside of it), I have invested serious time and money into ESO. However, we have to face reality: the game is slowly but surely dying. The first major blow will come with the release of GTA 6, and the final nail in the coffin might be Guild Wars 3.
As someone who loves this universe, I want to share what this game is missing and what could have saved its outdated combat and PvP systems. 
1. Combat Synergy: Moving from "One-Button Spams" to Combo Chains (Inspired by Conqueror’s Blade)The current combat feels rigid. Instead of abilities simply triggering a one-time effect with a cooldown, ESO desperately needs a dynamic combo and chain system bound to a single key. Inspired by the Glaive mechanics in Conqueror's Blade, abilities should flow as continuous animations based on timing:
1st Press: Triggers a wide, sweeping weapon animation.
2nd Press (Perfect Timing Window): Transitions smoothly into a heavy follow-up strike.
3rd Press: Executes a powerful finisher that breaks blocks or knocks enemies down.

Note: Players should still be able to animation-cancel out of this using a dodge roll.

In ESO, this would look like combining Critical Charge -> Uppercut -> Reverse Slash into a single, evolving skill slot with its respective morphs. 
The same should apply to buffs. Imagine combining Dragon Blood -> Wing Buffet -> Earthspike Mantle into a 32-second sequence. To maintain all three effects at maximum efficiency, you would need to re-cast the ability within a strict 28–30 second window. Missing the window reduces the buff's effectiveness by a percentage, which you can only restore in the next cycle. This would add actual skill expression to buff management.

citations.review_text: Tome points for the tamriel tomes system requiring you to do busy work objectives to get the carrot on a stick dangled in front of you is an asinine system, you should simply get tome points for doing any task in the game so you can play how you want to, not forced into the chore list thats worse than what existed before the tome system

1. This game is a gold-digger.
Players without DLCs or a subscription are able to find Scryable antiquities or treasure maps that require a DLCs/subscription to actually unlock. The treasure maps can't even be sold to a shopkeeper for gold.
The game floods your inventory with loot and then forces you to pay gold to increase your bag-space but subscribed users get twice the bag-space AND a crafting bag that holds all of your crafting resources.
It slows the roll of players not paying extra by requiring players to more than double their tome-points just to unlock the next page of their tamriel tomes.

2. This game is badly balanced thanks to the players complaining in PVP.
Every encounter in the game is either too easy or likely to kill you because of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mechanic that you were not warned an enemy had. Your character ends up terribly proportioned when it comes to skills because your skills don't level as fast as your character does and most of the skills aren't anything until you manage to max them out.
